The Shotted halibut Eopsetta grigorjewi attains a maximum total length of 60 centimeters [Li = 60 centimeters], a size that places it among the larger-bodied pleuronectiform flatfishes of the North Pacific. Females ultimately achieve an asymptotic wet body mass of 2100 grams [Wwi = 2100 grams], a value derived from field measurements of the largest individuals sampled during trawl surveys across the species' continental shelf habitat. In contrast, the wet weight at puberty for females is approximately 66.6 grams [Wwp = approximately 66.6 grams], corresponding to a total length of 19.5 centimeters [Lp = 19.5 centimeters] at the onset of gonadal development. This marked disparity between pubertal and ultimate body mass, exceeding an order of magnitude, suggests that a substantial portion of somatic growth occurs after the initiation of reproductive capability, a pattern common among iteroparous teleosts with indeterminate growth. Field records indicate that the length at which 50 percent of individuals become reproductively mature is consistent across the species' range, though slight regional variation has been noted in response to local thermal regimes and food availability.

Egg diameter in Eopsetta grigorjewi averages approximately 0.6 millimeters, from which the wet weight at birth is calculated to be 0.00011 grams [Wwb = 0.00011 grams] for a newly hatched yolk-sac larva. The egg incubation period, from fertilisation through eclosion, proceeds rapidly under the thermal conditions typical of the species' spawning grounds. At a stable water temperature of 8.8 °C [T = 8.8 °C], the age at birth is 14 days [ab = 14 days], a relatively brief developmental interval that reflects the small egg size and the consequent limited yolk reserves available to the endotrophic larva. Following chorion rupture, the yolk-sac larva enters a lecithotrophic phase during which it relies entirely on endogenous nutrition while undergoing critical early organogenesis, including the initial differentiation of the digestive tract and the formation of the pectoral fin buds. The timing of this hatching event is tightly coupled to thermal conditions; deviations of even a few degrees from this temperature can accelerate or delay emergence by several days, affecting larval survival.

Reproduction in this species occurs via broadcast spawning, with females releasing pelagic eggs during discrete seasonal events. Each spawning event yields a substantial fecundity of approximately 500,000 eggs per clutch, a high value commensurate with the large asymptotic body size. Females typically produce a single clutch each year, thereby concentrating annual reproductive effort into a relatively brief spawning window. The combination of high fecundity per event and low annual frequency is characteristic of many demersal flatfishes that capitalise on seasonal productivity pulses in their continental shelf environment. The eggs are transparent and slightly buoyant, dispersing with prevailing currents during the incubation period. Following spawning, adults provide no parental care, and the pelagic larval stage must locate suitable settlement habitat independently after the completion of metamorphosis.

The lifespan of the Shotted halibut has been documented from tag-recapture studies and otolith-based age estimation. At the same thermal regime of 8.8 °C [T = 8.8 °C] typical of its deep-water habitat, individuals attain a maximum longevity of 5475 days [am = 5475 days], equivalent to approximately 15 years. This extended lifespan, coupled with delayed maturation until roughly 19.5 centimeters in total length, positions the species as a moderate-lived, slow-to-mature iteroparous strategist within the Pleuronectidae. The oldest individuals, predominantly females, are found in the colder, deeper portions of the species' distribution, where reduced metabolic demands may contribute to slower somatic senescence. Validation of these age estimates using bomb radiocarbon dating has confirmed annual periodicity in otolith increment formation, lending confidence to longevity records. Males generally exhibit slightly shorter lifespans and smaller maximum sizes, though quantitative sex-specific mortality data remain limited.

Comparative physiological studies indicate that the growth trajectory of Eopsetta grigorjewi follows a decelerating pattern typical of flatfishes, with the species approaching an ultimate total length of 60 centimeters [Li = 60 centimeters] only after several years of sustained somatic expansion. The transition from the rapidly growing juvenile phase to the slower-growing adult phase coincides roughly with the attainment of sexual maturity at a wet weight of 66.6 grams [Wwp = 66.6 grams]. Juvenile individuals inhabit shallower, sandier substrates than adults, shifting to deeper waters as they approach the size at puberty. Dietary composition shifts accordingly, with smaller individuals preying primarily on amphipods and polychaetes, while larger, older fish incorporate increasing proportions of demersal fish into their diet. This ontogenetic niche shift likely reduces intraspecific competition and allows the species to exploit a broader range of benthic resources across its continental shelf habitat, contributing to its success as a commercially harvested flatfish in the Sea of Japan and the Sea of Okhotsk.
